front: In the strict sense, what is Linux, and what is userspace?
back: Linux is only the kernel. Userspace is everything else you touch: the shell, `ls`, editors, the desktop, libraries and servers.

front: What does the kernel do, and how do programs reach it?
back: It talks to the hardware (CPU, memory, disks, network cards) and decides which program runs when. Programs ask it for work through system calls.

front: Which parts together make up a Linux distribution?
back: A kernel, userspace software, an installer, a package manager and a release policy (how often new versions appear and how long they get updates).

front: Mira runs `uname -s` and then `uname -o`. What do the two commands ask for?
back: `uname -s` prints the kernel name, `Linux`. `uname -o` prints the operating system, `GNU/Linux`. The difference is exactly kernel versus whole system.

front: Which family do Debian, Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi OS belong to, and which package tools do they use?
back: The Debian-based family. Packages are `.deb` files, handled by `dpkg` (low level) and `apt` (high level).

front: Name the members of the Enterprise Linux family and its package tools.
back: RHEL, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux, Fedora Linux and CentOS Stream. Packages are `.rpm` files, handled by `rpm` and `dnf`.

front: Which distributions are SUSE-based, and which tool installs their packages?
back: SUSE Linux Enterprise (SLE), openSUSE Leap and openSUSE Tumbleweed. Packages are `.rpm` files; the high-level tool is `zypper`.

front: Ada wants a very small container image. Which distribution, using which libc, shell tools and package manager, is popular for that?
back: Alpine Linux. It uses musl instead of the GNU C library, BusyBox for its basic tools and `apk` for packages (`.apk` files).

front: Put Fedora, CentOS Stream and RHEL in order from newest software to commercial product.
back: Fedora comes first (upstream), CentOS Stream sits between, and RHEL is the commercial product you pay support for.

front: What are AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux?
back: Free, community-driven distributions that aim to be compatible with RHEL, so software built for RHEL runs on them. They suit people who don’t need Red Hat’s paid support.

front: In Debian, what is the difference between stable, testing and unstable?
back: Stable is the tested release for real work. Testing holds packages being prepared for the next stable. Unstable (nicknamed `sid`) is where new software arrives first.

front: What is a rolling release? Name two examples.
back: A release with no version numbers to upgrade between: you keep updating and always get the newest packages. Examples: openSUSE Tumbleweed and Alpine `edge`.

front: How often does Ubuntu release, and what makes an LTS release special?
back: A new release comes every six months. Every two years one is an LTS (Long-Term Support) release with five years of standard security maintenance.

front: Does a "stable" release mean it never crashes?
back: No. Stable means it changes little apart from security and bug fixes. It trades new features for predictability, which is why Ada picks it for the build server.

front: What is the difference between an alpha and a beta version?
back: Both are early test versions released before a version is declared ready. Alpha is rougher and earlier than beta.

front: Through which Debian lines does new software move before it ends up in a stable release?
back: It enters unstable, moves to testing, and the testing line becomes the next stable release.

front: Jonas says his Android phone runs Linux, so he can `apt install` things. Is that right?
back: Half right. Android uses the Linux kernel, but its userspace is not GNU: apps run in Android’s own runtime, and there is no `apt` and usually no ordinary shell.

front: Which distribution is the official system for Raspberry Pi boards, and what was it called before May 2020?
back: Raspberry Pi OS, based on Debian. It was called Raspbian before the Raspberry Pi Foundation renamed it.

front: Which distributions did the 010-160 exam list besides the families above, and which family is Linux Mint in?
back: Linux Mint (a beginner-friendly desktop based on Ubuntu and Debian, so Debian family), CentOS, Scientific Linux, Red Hat, SUSE and Raspbian.

front: What happened to CentOS Linux, and what took over its job?
back: The CentOS Project ended CentOS Linux (version 8 on 31 December 2021, version 7 on 30 June 2024). CentOS Stream continues the name; AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux became the free RHEL-compatible choices.

front: What is an embedded system? Why is Linux popular for it?
back: A small computer built into a device with one job, such as a router, TV or car dashboard. Linux is free, can be shrunk down and runs on many processor types.

front: Give three examples of embedded Linux, and say what the Raspberry Pi is.
back: A router, a TV and a smart thermostat. The Raspberry Pi is a general-purpose board that is a common base for embedded projects, like TuxPixel’s wall status screen.

front: What does "Linux in the cloud" mean?
back: Companies rent computing power (virtual servers, storage, databases) over the internet instead of buying machines. You choose a Linux image, start the server in minutes and pay for the time it runs.

front: Which operating system do most rented cloud servers run?
back: Linux. You pick a distribution as the image when you create the server.

front: Why do users of an embedded Linux device often not know Linux is inside?
back: The device has one fixed job and no visible desktop or shell. Linux is just the free, trimmed-down system underneath.

front: Why would Ada start a cloud server instead of buying a machine?
back: Cloud servers are rented over the internet: they start in minutes, you pay for the time they run, and you can remove them when done.

front: What does Android use from Linux, and what does it not use?
back: It uses the Linux kernel, built from upstream long-term-support kernels plus extra patches. It doesn’t use the usual GNU userspace.

front: Why is a typical Android phone not a Linux distribution in the desktop sense?
back: Its userspace is Android’s own: apps run in Android’s runtime, there is no package manager like `apt` and usually no ordinary shell for the user.
